meta.title: Who really said "Ladies and gentlemen of the class of '97: Wear sunscreen"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Kurt Vonnegut. The famous “sunscreen” line was written by Chicago Tribune columnist Mary Schmich, June 1, 1997, then hoaxed online as a Vonnegut MIT speech.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Ladies and gentlemen of the class of '97: Wear sunscreen'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Vonnegut — it’s Mary Schmich’s 1997 Chicago Tribune column, hoaxed into a fake MIT commencement address.

answer.label: Not Kurt Vonnegut — actually Mary Schmich
answer.authorDates: b. 1953 · Chicago Tribune columnist & Pulitzer Prize winner
answer.sourceLine: The line opens Mary Schmich’s column “Advice, like youth, probably just wasted on the young,” published in the Chicago Tribune on June 1, 1997 ↗. It was never spoken by Kurt Vonnegut — the essay went viral as a hoax email falsely billing it as his MIT commencement address, though MIT’s 1997 speaker was Kofi Annan and Vonnegut never spoke there.

docMeta.dd: “Advice, like youth, probably just wasted on the young”

source.excerpt: Ladies and gentlemen of the class of ’97: Wear sunscreen. If I could offer you only one tip for the future, sunscreen would be it. The long-term benefits of sunscreen have been proved by scientists, whereas the rest of my advice has no basis more reliable than my own meandering experience.
trail: The column ran in the Chicago Tribune on June 1, 1997 ↗; MIT later published Schmich’s own account of how her words were mistaken for Vonnegut’s.
Wikipedia ↗ documents the viral hoax email crediting Vonnegut and an MIT commencement that never happened.
Quote Investigator ↗ traces the column’s advice lines to Schmich and notes their later stray misattributions.
source.excerptNote: The column frames the piece with the line “Inside every adult lurks a graduation speaker dying to get out,” then delivers this mock commencement address.

source.rightsNote: First published in the Chicago Tribune on June 1, 1997, the column is well within copyright. Rights rest with Mary Schmich and the Tribune; Baz Luhrmann licensed the text (with Schmich’s permission and royalties) for his 1997–99 spoken-word song.

author.name: Mary Schmich
author.heading: Mary Schmich
author.metaLine: b. 1953 · Chicago Tribune columnist & 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary
author.bio: Mary Schmich is an American journalist who wrote a long-running column for the Chicago Tribune and won the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary. Her June 1, 1997 column — a mock graduation speech built around the advice to “wear sunscreen” — became one of the internet’s most famous texts after it was circulated as a Kurt Vonnegut speech. She also co-wrote the Brenda Starr comic strip for many years.

misattribution.heading: How Vonnegut got the credit
misattribution.intro: The “sunscreen” essay is one of the internet’s most famous misattributions — a genuine newspaper column that a viral 1997 email re-labeled as a Kurt Vonnegut commencement speech.

items.why: A chain email in 1997 circulated Schmich’s column as Vonnegut’s address to the MIT graduating class. He never gave it: MIT’s 1997 commencement speaker was Kofi Annan ↗, and Vonnegut had no involvement. He told reporters the words weren’t his — “it wasn’t my wittiness.”

items.scope: “Do one thing every day that scares you”
items.why: One advice line from the same column later drifted onto Eleanor Roosevelt. Quote Investigator ↗ found no evidence Roosevelt ever said it; Schmich wrote it in 1997.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Mary Schmich ↗, whose Chicago Tribune column of June 1, 1997 opens “Ladies and gentlemen of the class of ’97: Wear sunscreen.”

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: Schmich’s column was a deliberately light, self-deprecating mock commencement speech — “the rest of my advice has no basis more reliable than my own meandering experience.” Stripped of her byline and forwarded as a Kurt Vonnegut speech, it gained borrowed literary gravity that helped it circle the globe within weeks.

Baz Luhrmann set the text, word for word, to music in his 1997–99 track “Everybody’s Free (To Wear Sunscreen),” which topped the UK charts. Luhrmann credited Schmich, who granted permission and receives royalties — cementing her authorship even as the Vonnegut myth persisted.
context.pull: “Out in the lawless swamp of cyberspace, Mr. Vonnegut and I are one.” — Mary Schmich
